query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substitution of heavier elements with lighter ones in the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy will reduce its density without sacrificing its strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.conditions: Temperature range: room temperature to 1600 °C, Loading: yield strength and fracture toughness
generation.mechanism: Alloying and phase stability, with the formation of a solid solution and potentially a BCC + B2 microstructure
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced density by 5-10% while maintaining yield strength above 1500 MPa at room temperature and above 800 MPa at 1000 °C
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of 10.21 g cm−3, yield strength of 1600 MPa at room temperature, and 855 MPa at 1000 °C
generation.boundary: Temperature range: room temperature to 1600 °C, Loading: yield strength and fracture toughness
generation.uncertainty: The actual reduction in density and maintenance of mechanical properties may vary depending on the specific substitution ratio and processing conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Compression tests at room temperature and 1000 °C, density measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the substituted alloy exhibits a density reduction of less than 3% or a yield strength decrease of more than 10% at room temperature or 1000 °C, the hypothesis is falsified

To verify this novel alloy design strategy, an industrial scale AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 ingot of ~2.5 kg in weight was prepared, as shown in Fig. 1a . The bulk AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 alloy exhibited an excellent castability with few casting defects, significantly differentiating with other bulk HEAs. The tensile test specimen was machined from the bulk alloy ingot and is shown in Fig. 1b . The cast microstructure of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 is shown in Fig. 2a . Even in such a bulk cast ingot, a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure characteristic of eutectic alloys was achieved. The inter-lamellar spacing was about 2 μm. The coupled grown two phases showed a clear compositional contrast, with the regions marked by A in Fig. 2b were rich in Co, Cr and Fe, while the regions marked by B were rich in Al and Ni (detailed compositional information given in Table 1 ). An enlarged microstructure given in Fig. 2c shows that dense nanoscale NiAl-rich precipitates (marked as B II ) occurred in the CoCrFe-rich region. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . 3.1. Microstructure and Phase Evolution after SPS

The general microstructure of the HEA composite is shown in Figure 1 . The specimens are highly densified by the reaction sintering process without visible pores. The composite presented three obviously identifiable contrasts, namely light, grey, and black regions (marked as A, B, and C). The volume fraction of the light phase, grey phase, and black phase are 60.8%, 32.2%, and 7.0%, respectively. Since the content of carbon and oxygen cannot be measured accurately by EDS, EPMA experiment was employed to analyze the chemical composition in these areas ( Table 1 ). The results indicate that the region A consists of only 10.66 at. % Ti and 16.79 at. % Al, while Ti and Al atoms are enriched in the region B and C, respectively. Noticeably, the region C in Figure 1 was enriched in Al and O, indicating the formation of Al 2 O 3 .
